triage.name: Neonatal hypoglycemia
triage.reason: Infant of a diabetic mother or growth-restricted infant with jitteriness, lethargy or poor feeding; a very common problem diagnosed by bedside glucose with a broad differential.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Pallor' not found in SNOMED CT
presentation: term 'Pallor' not found in SNOMED CT
presentation: term 'Pallor' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Occurs in newborns; incidence is highest in preterm and small-for-gestational-age infants
More common in infants of diabetic mothers and in late-preterm infants
Seen in both term and preterm newborns

risk_factors.text: Small for gestational age or intrauterine growth restriction
Maternal beta-blocker or corticosteroid use near delivery

family_history: Family history of neonatal hypoglycemia or metabolic disorder

chief_complaints.text: My baby is shaky and jittery
My baby is sleepy and hard to wake for feeds
My baby is not feeding well
My baby's skin looks pale and sweaty

hpi.onset: Within the first hours to days of life, often in the first 24–48 hours
hpi.duration: Hours to days; may be transient or recurrent depending on cause
hpi.progression: Symptoms may be intermittent and worsen with feeding delays or stress; can progress to seizures or apnea if untreated
hpi.quality: Neurologic and autonomic signs such as jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, sweating, and pallor
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; can be asymptomatic or progress to seizures
hpi.timing: Often worse when feeding is delayed or during the first 1–2 days of life

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm and small-for-gestational-age infants may have no classic signs and are detected only by screening glucose; symptoms can be subtle such as temperature instability or apnea.
Not applicable; this condition occurs in newborns.

general.mild: Alert but jittery or easily startled; otherwise well-appearing
general.moderate: Lethargic and difficult to arouse for feeds; jittery when handled
general.severe: Poorly responsive, hypotonic, pale and sweaty; may have a seizure
general.critical: Unresponsive or actively seizing, apneic, pale and mottled

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant at rest and during handling; hold a limb gently to see if the tremor stops
findings.finding: Fine, rapid tremor of the limbs that is suppressed by gentle restraint

findings.maneuver: Observe alertness and attempt to arouse the infant for a feed
findings.finding: Reduced alertness, difficult to wake, poor feeding effort

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant's response to handling and feeding
findings.finding: High-pitched cry and excessive fussiness with handling

findings.maneuver: Assess limb and truncal tone with passive movement and ventral suspension
findings.finding: Reduced muscle tone; infant feels floppy

findings.maneuver: Observe for abnormal repetitive movements; if suspected, examine for subtle motor automatisms
findings.finding: Focal or generalized seizure activity, sometimes subtle (eye deviation, lip smacking, cycling movements)

findings.maneuver: Observe breathing pattern and respiratory effort
findings.finding: Pause in breathing lasting more than 20 seconds or with bradycardia/desaturation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin color in good light
findings.finding: Pale, mottled or dusky skin color
Diaphoresis, especially over the forehead and trunk

findings.maneuver: Measure axillary temperature with a low-reading thermometer
Palpate the anterior fontanelle with the infant upright and at rest
findings.finding: Anterior fontanelle is soft, flat and normal in size

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lungs and observe respiratory effort
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds, no grunting, retractions or tachypnea

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate peripheral pulses
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2, no murmur, regular rate and rhythm, strong peripheral pulses

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently palpate the abdomen
findings.finding: Soft, non-distended abdomen without tenderness or masses

labs.caveat: Bedside (heel-stick) glucose is the screening test; any value below 45 mg/dL in a newborn needs confirmation by a laboratory serum glucose before treatment is escalated. Values are lower in the first hours of life and in preterm infants.
Persistent lactic acidosis with hypoglycemia suggests sepsis, asphyxia or an inborn error of metabolism rather than simple transient hypoglycemia.
Low bicarbonate accompanies metabolic acidosis from sepsis, asphyxia or a metabolic disorder.
Order when hypoglycemia is persistent or recurrent, or when there is vomiting, lethargy or acidosis; hyperammonemia points to an inborn error of metabolism.
A low cortisol during hypoglycemia is inappropriately normal and suggests adrenal insufficiency or congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Congenital hypothyroidism can present with hypoglycemia and prolonged jaundice; part of the newborn screen.
Hypocalcemia commonly coexists in infants of diabetic mothers and in preterm or asphyxiated infants and can cause jitteriness on its own.
Hypomagnesemia can cause refractory hypocalcemia and jitteriness.
Polycythemia (venous hematocrit above 65%) causes hypoglycemia by increased glucose consumption and hyperviscosity.
Thrombocytopenia with hypoglycemia raises concern for sepsis or a congenital infection.
Leukocytosis or leukopenia supports sepsis, which both causes and complicates hypoglycemia.
Supports sepsis; may be normal early in neonatal infection.
Jaundice with hypoglycemia suggests hemolysis, sepsis or a metabolic disorder.
Low CSF glucose relative to serum supports meningitis; CSF glucose normally runs about two-thirds of serum glucose.
Pleocytosis supports meningitis or congenital infection as the cause of the hypoglycemia.
Elevated protein accompanies meningitis or congenital infection.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected intracranial hemorrhage or hypoxic-ischemic injury in a sick or seizing newborn

findings.text: Normal brain parenchyma and no hemorrhage
Diffuse increased echogenicity of white matter suggesting hypoxic-ischemic injury

imaging.preferred_when: Persistent seizures or suspected hypoglycemic brain injury after glucose is corrected

findings.text: Bilateral occipital and posterior parietal cortical and white matter injury
Restricted diffusion in the posterior cerebral regions on diffusion-weighted imaging

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected congenital heart disease or shock with hypoglycemia

initial.why: Bedside heel-stick glucose is the first test in any symptomatic or at-risk newborn; confirm any low value with a laboratory serum glucose
Looks for infection, polycythemia and thrombocytopenia
Assesses glucose, electrolytes, calcium and acid-base status
Hypocalcemia is a common coexisting cause of jitteriness in at-risk infants
Screens for sepsis, asphyxia or a metabolic disorder when hypoglycemia is persistent
Ordered with the initial sepsis evaluation in a symptomatic or unstable newborn
initial.only_if: sepsis is suspected (ill-appearing, temperature instability, risk factors)

initial.why: Lumbar puncture as part of the sepsis evaluation when meningitis is suspected
initial.only_if: meningitis or sepsis is suspected and the infant is stable enough for the procedure

confirmatory.why: Confirms an inborn error of metabolism when hypoglycemia is persistent or recurrent despite feeding
Confirms adrenal insufficiency when hypoglycemia is refractory with an inappropriately normal cortisol
Confirms congenital hypothyroidism when the newborn screen is abnormal or hypoglycemia persists

supporting.why: Supports sepsis as the underlying cause
Jaundice with hypoglycemia suggests hemolysis, sepsis or a metabolic disorder
Polycythemia is a treatable cause of neonatal hypoglycemia
Looks for hemorrhage or hypoxic-ischemic injury in a seizing or encephalopathic newborn
supporting.only_if: seizure, suspected intracranial hemorrhage or hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy

supporting.why: Defines hypoglycemic brain injury after glucose is corrected
supporting.only_if: persistent seizures or suspected brain injury

not_indicated.why: Reflects long-term glucose control and has no role in the newborn; maternal diabetes is assessed from the mother's history
Only if congenital heart disease or shock is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: suspected congenital heart disease or shock

not_indicated.why: Only if an adrenal cause is suspected

decision_points: Check a bedside glucose in every symptomatic newborn and in all at-risk infants (preterm, small or large for gestational age, infant of a diabetic mother) within the first hours of life
Confirm any low bedside glucose with a laboratory serum glucose before escalating treatment
Treat and recheck glucose within 30 minutes of any intervention; persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia needs a broader metabolic and endocrine workup
Draw the critical metabolic sample (lactate, ammonia, cortisol, insulin) before correcting glucose when an inborn error or hyperinsulinism is suspected
A seizing or apneic newborn is treated for hypoglycemia immediately while the workup proceeds

criteria.name: Neonatal hypoglycemia thresholds
criteria.summary: A newborn is considered hypoglycemic when the blood glucose is below about 45 mg/dL, with lower thresholds and closer monitoring in the first hours of life; values below 25–35 mg/dL are severe and require immediate treatment. Thresholds vary slightly by guideline and by whether the infant is symptomatic.
items: Bedside glucose below 45 mg/dL prompts confirmation and treatment
Symptomatic infants are treated at any low value
Persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia after feeding and IV glucose suggests hyperinsulinism or an inborn error of metabolism

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: Sepsis is both a cause and a mimic of neonatal hypoglycemia; both present with lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability and jitteriness in the first days of life.
differential.trigger: Ill-appearing, unstable temperature, or risk factors for infection (prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever, group B streptococcus colonization)

history: Maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis
Onset of poor feeding and lethargy rather than isolated jitteriness
Temperature instability (fever or hypothermia)
exam: Signs of shock (poor perfusion, prolonged capillary refill)
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia with left shift
Low CSF glucose with pleocytosis if meningitis

differential.name: Hypocalcemia of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Hypocalcemia causes jitteriness, tremors and irritability that look identical to hypoglycemia and frequently coexists in infants of diabetic mothers, preterm and asphyxiated infants.

history: Infant of a diabetic mother, preterm or asphyxiated infant
Jitteriness that persists after feeding and glucose correction
exam: May have prolonged QT on ECG
labs: Low serum calcium (below about 7 mg/dL in term infants)

differential.name: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Perinatal asphyxia causes lethargy, poor feeding, seizures and hypoglycemia, and is a common cause of neonatal encephalopathy.
differential.trigger: Sentinel event at delivery (shoulder dystocia, cord prolapse, placental abruption), low Apgar scores, or need for resuscitation

history: Sentinel event at delivery or difficult resuscitation
Low Apgar scores
Seizures in the first 24 hours
labs: Hypoglycemia may be present but is not the primary cause
imaging: Cranial ultrasound or MRI showing diffuse or posterior cerebral injury

differential.name: Inborn error of metabolism
differential.why_considered: Disorders of gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation and amino acid metabolism present with persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia, lethargy, vomiting and acidosis that does not resolve with feeding.
differential.trigger: Hypoglycemia that persists or recurs despite feeding and IV glucose, especially with vomiting, acidosis or a family history of neonatal death

history: Consanguinity or family history of neonatal death or metabolic disease
Symptoms worsen with fasting or illness
Vomiting and poor feeding
exam: Abnormal odor (e.g., maple syrup, sweaty feet)
labs: Abnormal newborn screen or plasma acylcarnitine profile

differential.name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycemia, lethargy, poor feeding and shock in the newborn period.
differential.trigger: Hypoglycemia with hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or ambiguous genitalia

history: Family history of congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Progressive lethargy and poor feeding over the first weeks
Vomiting

differential.name: Polycythemia of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Increased red cell mass causes hypoglycemia through increased glucose consumption and hyperviscosity, and presents with jitteriness, lethargy and poor feeding.

history: Infant of a diabetic mother, twin-twin transfusion, or delayed cord clamping
Plethora and poor feeding

differential.name: Congenital hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Congenital hypothyroidism can present with hypoglycemia, lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia and prolonged jaundice in the newborn period.

history: Prolonged jaundice
Constipation
Large fontanelle and macroglossia
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Congenital heart disease
differential.why_considered: Critical congenital heart disease can present with shock, poor feeding, lethargy and hypoglycemia in the first days of life.
differential.trigger: Cyanosis, murmur, weak pulses, or differential cyanosis with shock

history: Antenatal diagnosis of cardiac defect
Poor feeding and sweating with feeds
Cyanosis noted at home or in the nursery
labs: Hyperoxia test fails to raise PaO2

severity.mild: Asymptomatic or mildly jittery infant with a bedside glucose of 45–54 mg/dL; feeding well and otherwise well-appearing
severity.moderate: Lethargic, difficult to arouse for feeds, jittery when handled, with a glucose of 36–45 mg/dL; may have hypothermia or pallor
severity.severe: Poorly responsive, hypotonic, pale and sweaty, or with a seizure; glucose 25–36 mg/dL
severity.critical: Unresponsive or actively seizing, apneic, pale and mottled with glucose below 25 mg/dL; risk of hypoglycemic brain injury

red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoglycemia with risk of brain injury; treat immediately and confirm glucose
Critical hypoglycemia requiring immediate IV dextrose

red_flags.finding: Persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia despite feeding and IV glucose
red_flags.meaning: Suggests hyperinsulinism or an inborn error of metabolism; needs a metabolic workup
Consider sepsis, congenital heart disease or adrenal insufficiency
Points to an inborn error of metabolism

complications.name: Hypoglycemic brain injury
clues: Bilateral occipital and posterior parietal injury on MRI

complications.name: Seizures
clues: Subtle motor automatisms or eye deviation

complications.name: Developmental delay or neurodevelopmental impairment
clues: History of severe or recurrent neonatal hypoglycemia

complications.name: Recurrent hypoglycemia
clues: Hypoglycemia recurring after feeding and IV glucose

special_populations.differences: Preterm and small-for-gestational-age infants may have no classic signs and are detected only by screening glucose; symptoms can be subtle such as temperature instability or apnea. Thresholds are lower in the first hours of life and in preterm infants.
Not applicable; this condition occurs in newborns.
Maternal diabetes, beta-blocker or corticosteroid use near delivery increases the risk of neonatal hypoglycemia; infants of diabetic mothers are screened closely.

key_questions.question: When did the symptoms start, and how old is the baby now?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset within the first hours to 48 hours of life, consistent with the typical timing of neonatal hypoglycemia

key_questions.question: What exactly have you noticed — jitteriness, sleepiness, poor feeding, sweating, or a change in skin color?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic and autonomic signs such as jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, sweating or pallor

key_questions.question: Does the jitteriness stop when you gently hold the limb still?
key_questions.looking_for: Tremor suppressed by gentle restraint, which favors jitteriness over a true seizure

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any episodes of stiffening, eye deviation, lip smacking or cycling movements?
key_questions.looking_for: Subtle or overt seizures, which indicate severe hypoglycemia and risk of brain injury

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any pauses in breathing or turned blue?
key_questions.looking_for: Apnea, which occurs with severe hypoglycemia and also suggests sepsis

key_questions.question: How has feeding been going — is the baby waking for feeds and taking them well?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding or difficulty arousing for feeds, a common presenting sign and a cause of worsening hypoglycemia

key_questions.question: How many weeks was the baby born, and what was the birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm birth, small for gestational age or large for gestational age, all strong risk factors

key_questions.question: Did you have diabetes during pregnancy, and how was it managed?
key_questions.looking_for: Infant of a diabetic mother, the classic risk factor for neonatal hypoglycemia

key_questions.question: Were there any problems around delivery — a difficult delivery, low Apgar scores, or a need for resuscitation?
key_questions.looking_for: Perinatal stress or asphyxia, which causes hypoglycemia and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy

key_questions.question: Was the baby's temperature checked — has it been low?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypothermia, which both accompanies and worsens hypoglycemia and suggests sepsis

key_questions.question: Has the baby been ill-appearing, mottled, or felt cool and clammy?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of sepsis or shock, which must not be missed as a cause or complication

key_questions.question: What medications were you taking near the end of pregnancy, especially for blood pressure or to mature the baby's lungs?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal beta-blockers or corticosteroids, which increase the risk of neonatal hypoglycemia

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of low blood sugar in newborns, metabolic disease, or a baby who died in the newborn period?
key_questions.looking_for: An inborn error of metabolism or a familial form of hyperinsulinism

key_questions.question: Has the baby been vomiting or having any diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting suggests an inborn error of metabolism; diarrhea is uncommon and argues against it

key_questions.question: Has the baby had a fever or been unusually warm?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or temperature instability, which raises concern for sepsis

accepted_names: Low blood sugar in the newborn
reasoning_points: The infant is in the first hours to days of life, the typical window for neonatal hypoglycemia
Symptoms are neurologic and autonomic — jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, sweating, pallor, hypothermia — and are nonspecific
There is a strong risk factor such as maternal diabetes, prematurity, small or large for gestational age, or perinatal stress
A bedside heel-stick glucose is low (below about 45 mg/dL) and is confirmed with a laboratory serum glucose
The jitteriness is suppressed by gentle restraint, distinguishing it from a true seizure
Symptoms improve after feeding or glucose administration, supporting hypoglycemia as the cause
Persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia after feeding and IV glucose points to hyperinsulinism or an inborn error of metabolism
Look-alikes such as sepsis, hypocalcemia, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, congenital heart disease and adrenal insufficiency are considered and excluded

easy: Infant of a diabetic mother in the first 24 hours of life
Bedside glucose clearly low and confirmed on serum glucose
Symptoms resolve after feeding or IV dextrose
medium: Preterm or small-for-gestational-age infant with subtle signs such as temperature instability or apnea
Jitteriness that persists after glucose correction, suggesting coexisting hypocalcemia
Large-for-gestational-age infant with a normal exam but an abnormal screening glucose
hard: Asymptomatic at-risk infant detected only by protocol screening
Persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia despite feeding and IV glucose, suggesting hyperinsulinism or an inborn error of metabolism
Ill-appearing infant with hypoglycemia and shock, where sepsis or congenital heart disease is the real problem
Seizing newborn with subtle motor automatisms mistaken for benign jitteriness
Infant with hypoglycemia, vomiting and acidosis pointing to a metabolic disorder
